notes:
I could only cover a small part of the passage. My search and fetch limits ran out early, and the Enduring Word chapter page came back empty. So I have nothing on vv. 1–2, 11–22 (Pilate, Barabbas, Pilate's wife and the crowd) and nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, Pentecostal or popular-teaching sites. What I have centres on vv. 3–10, and most of it is about v. 9. Another round of searches would be needed for the rest.

---

**v. 3–5: Judas's remorse and death**

- Matthew Henry (Concise) says Judas fully admitted to the chief priests that he had sinned and betrayed an innocent man. Henry treats that admission as a witness to Christ's innocence. In his reading, Judas hanged himself because he could not bear the terror of God's anger and his own despair. Henry also thinks Judas almost certainly died before Jesus did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- Henry's verdict is that Judas came close to repentance, but not the kind that saves: he confessed to men, not to God. Henry warns readers not to settle for this kind of half-conviction, which leaves pride and rebellion in place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm

**v. 4: "What is that to us?"**

- Henry sees the rulers as hardened. They had paid for this innocent man's blood, yet they shrugged it off. He calls this a picture of people mocking sin, and of how we downplay our own sin by pointing at other people's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm

**v. 7–8: The potter's field and the Field of Blood**

- Henry notes that many interpreters see the burial ground for foreigners as a picture of Christ's blood bringing mercy to outsiders and Gentile sinners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- Bible Hub's verse notes link this to Acts 1:18–19, where the field is called *Akeldama*, "Field of Blood." They say the betrayal money paying for a cemetery is a lasting reminder of how far sin will go. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-9.htm

**v. 9–10: Why "Jeremiah," when the words are close to Zechariah 11:12–13?**

Interpreters have long argued over this verse. The StudyLight commentary *Light of Israel* says it has caused interpreters "enormous problems" over the centuries. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-9.html

How the older commentators explain it:

- **Jeremiah stood first among the prophets** (Barnes; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, following Lightfoot). In some old Jewish orderings, Jeremiah's book came first in the collection of the Prophets. Matthew may simply be citing that whole collection by the name at its head, the way Jesus used "the Psalms" for the whole group of writings in Luke 24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- **A copyist's slip** (Barnes, Benson, Geneva Study Bible). Barnes thinks this the most likely answer: in abbreviated Greek, the two names differ by a single letter. The Reformation-era Geneva notes (Reformed) say the name slipped in through a scribe's error or someone's ignorance. They add that Matthew follows the prophet's meaning rather than his exact words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- **Jeremiah spoke it first and Zechariah wrote it down** (Grotius, as reported by Benson, a Methodist commentator). On this view the saying was passed down by Jewish tradition, and Matthew was right to credit Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- **Two prophecies blended together.** Bible Hub's Q&A says the thirty coins come from Zechariah, while the potter and the field echo Jeremiah 18–19 and 32. On this view Matthew names the better-known prophet to cover the whole set of allusions. https://biblehub.com/q/why_attribute_zechariah's_prophecy_to_jeremiah.htm
- **Quoting from memory** (Ellicott, Anglican). Ellicott weighs the other options. He finds this the most natural one: Matthew remembered Jeremiah's potter chapters and grouped this saying with them. His quotation doesn't match the Greek or Hebrew of Zechariah exactly, which supports the idea. Ellicott also says Zechariah's words have their own meaning in their original setting. For Matthew, it was enough that the old words fitted the events. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- **Meyer** (a 19th-century German scholar) calls the name simply a slip of memory and cites Augustine on the point. He describes the quotation as a very free adaptation of Zechariah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- **Gill** (Baptist) grants that "Jeremiah" is in all the Greek manuscripts and most ancient translations, though the Syriac and Persian versions just say "the prophet." He then lists ways people have tried to reconcile it. One is Jerome's report of reading these exact words in a Hebrew apocryphal book of Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm

**v. 9: "The price set on Him"**

- Barnes explains that "valued" here means "priced," not "esteemed." Thirty pieces of silver was the usual price of a slave. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-9.htm
- Bible Hub's notes connect this to Exodus 21:32, the payment owed when an ox gored a slave. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-9.htm
- One Bible Hub Q&A says the coins were probably Tyrian shekels, worth about four months' wages for a labourer. It also says that by paying a slave's price, the leaders effectively ranked Jesus as no more valuable than a slave. https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_30_silver_coins.htm

**Where traditions differ:** The sources disagree mainly on v. 9. The Reformed Geneva notes and Barnes blame a copyist. Benson, the Methodist, leans to a passed-down saying of Jeremiah or to the "Jeremiah stood first" view. Ellicott, the Anglican, prefers quoting from memory, and argues against assuming every inspired word must be literally exact. I didn't find teachers from these traditions disagreeing over any other verse here.
